title: Neurons speak to immune cells
objective: Explain how sensory neurons signal to immune cells via neuropeptides.

steps.title: An efferent role for sensory neurons
steps.body: Sensory neurons don't only send signals *in* — their peripheral endings can release **[[neuropeptide|neuropeptides]]** like **[[CGRP]]** and **[[substance P]]** locally. These act on nearby immune cells, so a [[nociceptor]] can actively shape the immune response, not just report pain.

steps.prompt: How can a sensory nociceptor influence local immunity?
options: By releasing neuropeptides from its endings onto nearby immune cells
By engulfing and digesting bacteria the way a macrophage does
By producing antibodies directed against the pathogen itself
By carrying its pain signal to the brain, which then dispatches immune cells
steps.explanation: Nociceptor endings release CGRP and substance P, which act on immune cells — an efferent, immune-modulating role for a 'sensory' neuron.

variants.setup: A nociceptor ending releases CGRP into inflamed tissue.
options: It acts on nearby immune cells
It directly kills the pathogen itself
It generates antibodies on the spot
variants.reveal: Released neuropeptides act on immune cells — neurons shaping immunity.

steps.title: Two directions at once
steps.body: The same neuron can carry a signal centrally *and* release neuropeptides peripherally. So 'afferent' doesn't mean 'input only' — these cells are nodes in a two-way neuroimmune conversation (the next units trace both directions).
